text: I went down to {name}. At this hour the place was down to the people who had nowhere better to be, and the bartender was letting the clock decide when that was.
{NameSubj} had the lights low and the radio lower. The smoke had settled at about hat height and stayed there, like it paid rent.
I found {name}. You knock, somebody looks at you through a slot, and then you’re in, which is how the whole city works if you know the knock.
{NameSubj} was still going. The band had stopped and the talk hadn’t, and the doorkeeper had the look of a man who counts heads for a living.
I went to {name}. The supper crowd had gone and the late crowd had come, and they were eating soup as if it were a decision.
{NameSubj} was half empty and fully lit, with the chairs going up on the far tables one by one.
I went in at {name}. The last show was running to a house of about a dozen, and the dark smelled of peanuts and wet coats.
{NameSubj} was showing a picture about a man who solved things in an hour and a half. I didn’t stay for the end. I never believe it anyway.
{NameSubj} was four floors of rooms and one landlady, and the landlady was the part that mattered. The hall smelled of cabbage and floor polish, in that order.
I went up the stoop at {name}. Every door in the hall had a lodger behind it and a landlady in front of it.
{Name}. The police had been and gone, and left the door shut and the light on, which is about what the police leave.
I went up to {name}. The stairs had been climbed by a lot of policemen tonight, and they hadn’t wiped their feet.
{NameSubj} was a tidy place with one thing missing, and the whole room knew which.
I went up to {name}. It was the kind of parlour where everything has a doily, including the doilies.
{NameSubj} had shut for the night, but there was a light in the back and somebody behind the counter who hadn’t gone home.
I went round to {name}. Work places at night have the same look as theatres in the day: everything ready, nothing happening.
{NameSubj} worked all night, which is more than I can say for most of the city. The light was hard and the coffee was harder.
I found {name}. It was the kind of place people go to so they can say they were somewhere else.
{NameSubj} didn’t have a sign, which was the sign. Somebody let me in and then looked at me as if they’d made a mistake.
I went round to {name}. Two rooms and a kitchen behind a door with three locks, two of them for show.
I went round to {name}, two rooms up a back stair with a cat on every landing.
Back at {place}. Nothing had moved but the clock.
I went back to {place}. It was the same place, a little later, which is all most places are.
{Place} again. The welcome was about what it had been the first time.
I walked back to {place}. The street was emptier, and so was I.
{Victim} was where they’d found him, in the chair by the table, as if he’d sat down to wait for something and it had come.
{Victim} was in the chair by the table, with his head on his arms, like a man asleep over his accounts.
{Victim} was on the floor between the table and the door. Nobody had covered him yet, and nobody had closed his eyes.
{Victim} was face down by the door, where he’d turned his back on somebody. It’s the one thing in this city you never do.
{Client} stood in the doorway of the parlour and looked at the place where {thing} ought to be, which is a thing you can do for a long time without it helping.
{Client} showed me in and stood by the spot where {thing} had been, the way people stand by a grave.

There were two glasses on the table. One smelled of rye and nothing else. The other smelled of rye and something sweet and chemical, like a hospital left out in the sun. Under the table, where it had rolled, was an empty brown bottle with a paper label from {x}. The lodgers there keep it on the hall shelf. {victim} had been drinking with somebody he knew.

A revolver lay under the chair, one chamber fired. I knew whose it was before I looked: it belongs in the hall-stand drawer at {x}, and the whole block knows it, because the landlady shows it to anybody who’s late with the rent. {victim} had been shot from across his own table.

A carving knife lay on the floor by the door. The handle had a mark burnt into it, the mark every knife in the kitchen at {x} has so that nobody walks off with one. Somebody had. {victim} had opened the door to somebody and turned his back.

A cup of cocoa sat on the table, gone cold and bitter at the bottom. Beside it was a brown bottle with a chemist’s label made out to {x}. Somebody had made {victim} cocoa, which is a kind thing to do, and then made sure it was the last.
There were two glasses on the table, and one of them smelled sweet and chemical. Under the table was an empty brown bottle with a surgery label on it: {x}.
There were two glasses on the table, and one of them smelled sweet and chemical. Under the table was an empty bottle with a {x} label, the kind that comes off the dispensary shelf.
A revolver lay under the chair, one chamber fired, with a pledge ticket from {x} still tied to the trigger guard. Somebody had redeemed it without paying.
A glass on the table smelled of bitter almonds, and beside it was a darkroom bottle labelled {x}. Photographers use the stuff to fix their prints. It fixes other things too.
{empty} The door was still unlocked, and there wasn’t a mark on it. Whoever it was had walked straight in.
{empty} The lock’s tongue was still taped back, the way it had been since Tuesday, and the door hadn’t a mark on it.
{empty} The key was back under the mat, and the door hadn’t a mark on it. Whoever it was had let themselves in and put the key back after, which is manners of a kind.
{empty} The parlour window was up six inches, and there was soot on the sill from the fire escape.
{empty} The key was back under the mat, and there wasn’t a mark on the door. Whoever it was had known exactly where to look.
{empty} The parlour window was up six inches, and there was soot on the sill from the fire escape. Whoever it was had known which window.
{empty} There wasn’t a mark on the door or the window. Whoever came in had a key.
{empty} The door had been locked again behind whoever it was, and there wasn’t a mark on it. Whoever it was had a key.
There was a page on each of them in there, in a small tidy hand. The one on top was {top}’s: {motive}.
He’d kept a page on each of them, the way a grocer keeps a slate. The one on top was {top}’s, and it said {motive}.
I went down to {name}. Upstairs the hat shop had gone dark, and down here the lamps were low and the talk was lower, the way it gets after midnight when the loud things have all been said.
{NameSubj} had a door you had to knock on, which on {street} is a formality. Everybody knows the knock, and the hats in the window upstairs have heard it so often they could do it themselves.
I went into {name}. It was a long narrow room with a brass rail worn bright where the feet go, and at this hour most of the feet had gone home.

{NameSubj} had its windows painted green up to the height of a hat, so that {street} could see the lights were on and nothing else. Inside it smelled of beer and a radiator working harder than it was paid to.
I went in at {name}. It was an old high room with a tin ceiling and a long mahogany bar, and the sawdust on the floor had collected the whole day in it: ash, peanut shells and bottle caps.
{NameSubj} was the oldest bar on {street} and acted like it. The sawdust gets changed on Mondays whether it needs it or not, and it always needs it.
I went to {name}. The cigars in the front window had been there so long they had gone the colour of the window, and nobody minded, because nobody came for the cigars.
{NameSubj} was one room with no windows, a curtain for a door and a bar along one wall. After midnight it had the quiet of a place that expects to be quiet and is paid to be.

I went to {name}, through the steam of the laundry and down a flight of stone steps. The band had packed up for the night, and the talk had got quieter and closer, the way talk does in a cellar after midnight.
{NameSubj} smelled faintly of starch, which is more than any other club in the city can say. The lantern over the bandstand was blue, as promised, and so was most of the music.
I went up the outside stair to {name}. The garage underneath was shut for the night, but the room still smelled of motor oil under the perfume and the cigarettes.

{NameSubj} had a floor that shook when anybody danced and a bandstand nobody was using. When a truck backed in downstairs, every glass in the room went up half an inch and came down again, and nothing spilled. They’d had practice.
I went down to {name}. The place smelled of garlic and grilled meat, there was a seltzer bottle on every table, and the piano in the corner had a cloth over it for the night.
{NameSubj} was still serving at this hour, because on {street} nobody goes home until they’ve argued about something over a plate of food. The garlic in the air was thick enough to lean on.
I went to {name}. The tables were marble, the tea came in glasses, and the mirrors on every wall made the room look three times the size it was.
{NameSubj} was where the theatre went to talk about itself after the curtain came down. The walls were covered in signed photographs, all of them smiling, none of them paying.
I went into {name}. It was dark wood and white tablecloths, with the grill at the back cooling down and ticking to itself.
{NameSubj} had served steaks to three generations of men whose doctors had told them to stop. The doctors were right, and so were the steaks.
I went in at {name}. The last show had let out, the screen was a big grey blank, and the rows were full of peanut shells and dropped programmes.
{NameSubj} had stopped the pictures for the night. Without one, a picture house is just three hundred red seats staring at a wall, which describes most of my evenings.
I went to {name}. It was a narrow little house with a ticket window the size of a letter box and a smell of floor polish and oranges.
{NameSubj} had its lobby lights on and a poster outside for a picture with a horse in it. {Place} only books pictures with horses in them, on the theory that a horse never gave a bad performance.
I went in at {name}. The play was over, but the stage still had its painted village up, a little wooden town waiting under one work light for the next performance.
{NameSubj} had let out, and the lobby still smelled of the audience: wool, oranges and opinions. The posters by the door promised a family tragedy in four acts, with songs.
I went up to {name}. The switchboards ran the length of the room, each one a wall of little holes and brass plugs, and the whole floor hummed with a low, steady “Number, please.”
{NameSubj} never closes, because somebody in this city always wants to talk to somebody else at the wrong hour. The little lights on the boards came on and went out all the time.
I went round to {name}. The ovens were going full blast, and the heat came out to meet me at the door like a relative.
{NameSubj} was the warmest room on {street} and the busiest. There was flour on everything, the floor, the walls and the light bulbs, and the first trays of rolls were coming out brown.
I went up to {name}. It was a big room of desks, green lamps and typewriters, with tomorrow’s newspaper being argued into shape one page at a time.
{NameSubj} ran on coffee, cigarettes and other people’s bad news. The floor was ankle deep in carbon paper and cigarette ends, and nobody had the time to mind.
I went up to {name}. The bank downstairs was dark, and the waiting room had its lamps half on and its magazines squared up, ready for tomorrow’s patients.
{NameSubj} was shut for the night, with the blinds down and the lamp lit in the waiting room. It smelled of clove oil and carbolic soap, the two smells of somebody being brave.
I went round to {name}. The blinds were down, but the big glass jars in the window, one red and one green, were still lit from behind, the way a pharmacy keeps a light on for the sick.
{NameSubj} was shut, with a hand-lettered sign in the door saying to ring in an emergency. Every pharmacy has that sign, and every pharmacist hopes you won’t.

I went to {name}. The three gold balls over the door had gone dull under the street lamp, and the window behind the grille was full of other people’s things: a banjo, a set of false teeth, a christening cup.
{NameSubj} was shut, with the grille pulled across the window and a light on somewhere at the back. Everything in a pawnshop is waiting for somebody to come back for it, and mostly nobody does.
I went up to {name}. The window downstairs was full of brides and babies and soldiers in frames, all of them looking out at the street as if somebody had just said something nice.
{NameSubj} was shut for the night. The studio had a painted garden on the back wall and a velvet chair in front of it, for people to look their best in.
I went up the stoop at {name}. It was four floors of narrow rooms and one long stair, with a gas lamp on each landing turned down to a little blue bead.
{NameSubj} smelled of boiled cabbage and lye soap, and the stairs creaked a different note on every step.
I went to {name}. It was a narrow brick house with a holy picture in the hall and a smell of beetroot soup that had got into the walls and settled.
{NameSubj} had its hall lamp lit and its floors scrubbed white. A sign by the stair asked for quiet in two languages, both of them firm.
I went up to {name}. They were named after the grand restaurant uptown, and the only thing they had in common with it was fish.
{NameSubj} were up a steep stair from {street}, three floors of them. The market below was shut and its stalls hosed down, but the smell of fish hadn’t gone anywhere.
I went to {name}. It was a tall thin house that leaned a little on its neighbour, like a lodger who has had one too many.
{NameSubj} was quiet at this hour. The hall smelled of paprika and floor wax, and a lamp had been left on at the turn of the stair.
I went up to {name}. It was a bare room under one green-shaded lamp, with a round table, a lot of chairs and the smell of cigars and cold coffee that a poker game leaves behind.
{NameSubj} had no sign and no name on the door, only a light under it. A gambling room doesn’t advertise. The people who need it always find it.
I went round to {name}. It was warm from the ovens, with sacks of flour along one wall and a table by the other where people paid a nickel to bet on a three-figure number in the illegal lottery.
{NameSubj} smelled of rye bread and pencil shavings. A bakery makes its money in the morning, and the back room made its money all night, a nickel at a time.
I went through to {name}. It was a small room with a roll-top desk, a framed portrait of somebody important and a big iron safe with the club’s eagle painted on the door.
{NameSubj} was where the club did the business it didn’t do in the front room. There were a lot of chairs for an office, and not much paper.
I went into {name}. It was a long bright room of little glass doors, each with a sandwich or a slice of pie behind it, and a nickel would open any one of them.
{NameSubj} was lit like an operating room and about as cosy. Nobody cooks for you at an Automat: somebody you never see puts the pie behind the glass, and you’re never introduced.
I went in at {name}. It was a big shabby picture house with the gilt coming off the plaster, and the back row sat under the balcony, where the light from the screen never quite reached.
{NameSubj} was the darkest place on {street} you could sit for a dime. That’s what the back row is for, and the management has known it for years.
I went in at {name}. The presses were running with a noise like a train going over a long bridge, and everything in the room smelled of ink and hot oil.
{NameSubj} printed what the city would read at breakfast, and the presses made sure nobody in the building slept through it. You had to shout to say good evening, so nobody did.
I went up to {name}. The stair smelled of the drugstore underneath, cherry syrup and camphor, and the light was still on behind the door at the top, where the police had left it.
{NameSubj} was one room at the top of the stairs. The police had been and gone, and the room had the look rooms get when a lot of people have stood in them and nobody sat down.
I climbed to {name}. The drugstore below was dark, and the only sound in the building was the stair under my feet.
I went up to {name}. The bakery downstairs had its ovens going, and the warm smell of bread came up through the floorboards, which didn’t seem right, and wasn’t anybody’s fault.
{NameSubj} were up a stair the police had worn a path in tonight. The door was shut and the light was on, the way they leave things.
I went up to {name}. Two rooms, a front and a back, with the police gone and the radiator still knocking, as if nobody had told it.
I climbed to {name}. Each flight was a little darker than the one under it, and at the top there was a door with the light still on behind it.
{NameSubj} was as high up as the building went. The police had been and gone, and left the place with its lamp lit and its door shut, like a shop on a holiday.
I went up to {name}. By the top floor I had a stitch in my side and an opinion about stairs, and the opinion was not kind.
I went in by the tailor’s passage to {name}. The shop was dark, and the dummies stood about in half-made jackets like a committee nobody had told the meeting was off.
{NameSubj} were at the back, past the cutting table and the steam press. The police had left the lamp lit and the door pulled to.
I went to {name}. The passage from {street} smelled of pressed wool and machine oil, and it ended at a door the police had pulled shut on their way out.
I went up to {name}. The stair carpet was worn to the threads in the middle, and the door at the top had a brass knocker that somebody polished every Saturday whether it needed it or not.
{NameSubj} was neat as a pin and twice as sharp about it. There were lace mats on every chair back and photographs on every wall, looking down at me as if I’d come in with my boots on.
I went to {name}. It was a good flat for {street}, with a carpet in the hall and lace on every table, kept the way people keep things they have finished paying for.
I went up the stoop to {name}. It was the good floor of a good old house, with high ceilings and furniture that had come down through the family and wasn’t going any further.
{NameSubj} was two tall rooms with folding doors between them, a thick carpet and a smell of beeswax.
I went to {name}. The house was old and proud of it, with a carpet on the stairs held down by brass rods, and every rod shone.
I went up to {name}. The delicatessen downstairs was shut, but the smell of pickles and smoked fish came up the stairs with me and stayed for the visit.
{NameSubj} was three small rooms kept very clean, with oilcloth on the kitchen table and a calendar from the delicatessen on the wall.
I went up to {name}. A narrow stair, a landing with one door on it, and on the door a nameplate that somebody had polished thin.
I went round to {name}. It was a walk-up like every walk-up on {street}: a hall that smelled of other people’s suppers and a stair with a bend in it.
{NameSubj} was two rooms and a kitchen at the top of the stairs, behind a doormat that had given up saying welcome years ago.
I went round to {name}. They were up two flights at the back, the kind of rooms people take when they mean to move somewhere better next year, and the year after.
{NameSubj} were up a back stair, with a lamp on the landing and a name written on a slip of paper and pinned to the door.
{Place} hadn’t changed while I was gone, which is the nicest thing a place can do for you.
I went back to {place}, which had kept my welcome at about room temperature.
Back at {place}, everything was where I’d left it except the time.
I came back into {place} the way you come back to a crossword, hoping it had got easier while I was out.
{Place} again, a little later and a little quieter.
I let myself back into {place}, and nobody made a fuss about it.
I walked back to {place} with my hands in my pockets and my questions in order.
{Place} looked the same the second time, which in my line of work is never quite true.
I went back to {place}, because there’s no such thing as a place you’re finished with.
{Place} was where I’d left it, and I was grateful, because I wasn’t sure where I’d left anything else tonight.
{Victim} was in the chair by the table, where the police had left him, with his chin down on his chest like a man who meant to rest his eyes for a minute.
{Victim} sat in his chair with his hands in his lap. If you didn’t know, you’d have said he was asleep, and lowered your voice.
{Victim} was in the chair with his head back and his mouth a little open, the way a man sleeps when he’s too tired to care how he looks.
{Victim} was slumped in the chair with one arm hanging down, as if sleep had come over him in the middle of a sentence.
{Victim} was in his chair, sitting very still, the way nobody living ever sits for long.
{Victim} was in the chair with his head to one side, like a man dozing over the evening paper, except that nobody dozes that still.
{Victim} was on the floor on his back, with one arm flung out and his eyes on the ceiling.
{Victim} lay on the floor where he’d fallen, on his side, with his knees drawn up a little.
{Victim} was on the floor in the middle of the room. A man looks smaller on the floor than he ever did standing up.
{Victim} lay by the door with his back to the room, as if he’d been on his way somewhere and been stopped.
{Victim} was face down just inside the door, with his back to the room, the way he must have been standing when it happened.
{Victim} lay by the door on his face. Nobody had moved him, and nobody had wanted to.
{Client} showed me in and stood by the place where {thing} belonged, holding {thing}’s dish as if it might be wanted any minute.
{Client} kept looking from the empty place to me and back, as if I might have {thing} in my coat.
{Client} had left everything just as it was, so that {thing} would know the way home.
{Client} took me straight to the place where {thing} had been and stood beside it like a museum guard with nothing left to guard.
{Client} showed me where {thing} had been kept and touched the place once, lightly, the way you touch a sore tooth.
“That’s where {thing} lives,” {client} said, and then, more quietly, “lived.”
Over the bar at {place} hung a mirror gone cloudy at the corners, which is the kindest way to be looked at after midnight.

prop.text: a mirror gone cloudy at the corners
pay: I caught myself in the cloudy mirror on the way out and decided not to ask.
The mirror behind the bar went on being kind to everybody, me included.
Even the cloudy mirror couldn’t make the night look any better, and it had been trying for years.

text: A brass spittoon stood at the foot of the bar at {place}, polished brighter than anything else in the room.

prop.text: a brass spittoon polished brighter than anything else in the room
pay: The spittoon still shone at the foot of the bar. That room had its priorities.
On the way out I nodded to the spittoon. It was the only thing in the place that had kept its shine.
The spittoon caught the light as I left, which is more attention than I got.

text: Behind the bar at {place} a moose head with one glass eye looked out over the bottles, having seen it all and liked none of it.

prop.text: a moose head with one glass eye
pay: The moose watched me go with its one good eye. I didn’t blame it.
The moose over the bottles hadn’t changed its opinion of me, and I hadn’t changed mine.
I said good night to the moose. It was the best listener in the room.

text: There was a radio on a shelf behind the bar at {place}, playing dance music so softly it might have been coming from next door.

prop.text: a radio playing dance music very softly
pay: The radio was still playing dance music for nobody who was dancing.
Somewhere on the radio a band was having a better night than I was.
The radio played on, low and cheerful, as if nothing had happened, which for the radio was true.

text: A glass globe hung from the ceiling at {place} with half its little mirrors gone, turning slowly over the dance floor.

prop.text: a glass globe with half its little mirrors gone
pay: The globe was still turning overhead, throwing light at a dance floor that had stopped asking for it.
I looked up at the globe on the way out. It had lost half its mirrors and kept going, which I respected.
The globe turned once more and caught me in a spot of light, the only spotlight I was going to get.

text: A saxophone lay on a chair on the empty bandstand at {place}, like a guest who had dozed off at the party.

prop.text: a saxophone lying on a chair on the bandstand
pay: The saxophone was still asleep on its chair. I envied it.
I went past the saxophone on its chair and didn’t wake it.
The saxophone on the bandstand had nothing to say, and said it beautifully.

text: A row of paper lanterns was strung across {place}, faded from red to pink by years of smoke.

prop.text: a string of paper lanterns faded to pink
pay: The paper lanterns swayed a little as the door went, pink and tired, like the rest of us.
I left under the paper lanterns. They’d seen worse nights, and they looked it.
The lanterns went on being cheerful about nothing in particular.

text: There was a coat-check window at {place} with a bell on the counter and a sign that said Not Responsible.

prop.text: a coat-check window with a sign that says Not Responsible
pay: Not Responsible, said the sign at the coat check. It was the most honest thing in the room.
I read the coat-check sign again on the way out. Not Responsible. I’d have liked one for myself.
The coat-check sign was still disowning everything. Some nights I know the feeling.

text: A cash register the size of a church organ stood by the door at {place}, all brass curls and little glass windows.

prop.text: a cash register the size of a church organ
pay: The brass register by the door sat waiting to ring, like an organ before the hymn.
I went out past the brass register, which looked at my coat and didn’t think much of it.
The register by the door gleamed. In a place like that, the money gets the best seat.

text: On every table at {place} there was a seltzer bottle in a wire cage, standing up straight like a guardsman.

prop.text: a seltzer bottle in a wire cage on every table
pay: The seltzer bottles stood at attention on every table, ready for a war that never came.
I nodded to the nearest seltzer bottle. It didn’t nod back. They’re trained not to.
The seltzer bottles were still on guard as I went out, which made one of us.

text: A big samovar sat at the end of the counter at {place}, steaming quietly to itself.

prop.text: a big samovar steaming at the end of the counter
pay: The samovar went on steaming at the end of the counter, the only thing in the room in no hurry at all.
I could have used a glass from the samovar. I could have used a lot of things.
The samovar hissed once as I passed, as if it had an opinion.

text: The day’s specials were chalked on a slate by the door at {place}, and the soup had been crossed out.

prop.text: a slate of the day’s specials with the soup crossed out
pay: The soup was still crossed out on the slate. Some things you find out too late.
I read the slate by the door again on the way out. Still no soup, which seemed about right for the night.
The slate by the door promised a lot and had crossed out the best of it, like most menus and most evenings.

text: A life-size cardboard cowboy stood in the lobby at {place}, fading, and tipping his hat at the box office.

prop.text: a life-size cardboard cowboy in the lobby
pay: The cardboard cowboy tipped his hat as I left. He’d been doing it all week to everybody.
I passed the cardboard cowboy. He had the look of a man who solves everything in the last reel.
The cardboard cowboy was still smiling in the lobby. It’s easy to smile when you’re cardboard.

text: A big brass ashtray full of sand stood by the inner doors at {place}, with a neat pattern raked into the sand.

prop.text: a brass ashtray of raked sand
pay: The sand in the brass ashtray had been raked smooth again. Order gets kept where it can be.
I put my cigarette out in the brass ashtray and spoiled the pattern. It was that kind of night.
The ashtray by the doors went on standing guard over its sand. Everything needs a job.

text: Above the lobby doors at {place} a painted plaster mask grinned down at everybody who came in, with the tip of its nose missing.

prop.text: a plaster theatre mask missing the tip of its nose
pay: The plaster mask over the doors was still grinning. It hadn’t heard a thing.
I looked up at the mask on the way out. Missing the tip of its nose and still grinning: a professional.
The plaster mask grinned me out of the door, the way it grins everybody out.

text: The lobby carpet at {place} was red and gold swirls, worn down to the threads in a path from the door to the seats.

prop.text: a red and gold carpet worn to the threads down the middle
pay: I walked out along the worn path in the carpet. I was adding to it.
The path in the lobby carpet was a little more worn than when I came in. I’d done my bit.
The worn path in the lobby carpet led out as well as in, which was the best news I’d had.

text: A holy picture hung in the hall at {place}, with a little lamp in a red glass under it.

prop.text: a holy picture with a red lamp under it
pay: The red lamp under the holy picture was still burning, for whoever needed it most.
I passed the holy picture on the stairs and kept my eyes front. I don’t like being looked at that kindly.
The holy picture watched me down the stairs with an expression I couldn’t afford.

text: On the landing at {place} a rubber plant had grown up to the ceiling and was thinking about going further.

prop.text: a rubber plant that had grown to the ceiling
pay: The rubber plant on the landing put a leaf on my hat as I passed. It was the friendliest thing in the house.
The rubber plant was still growing on the landing. At least something in that house was getting somewhere.
I went past the rubber plant on the landing. It had ambitions. I had a notebook.

text: A framed sign in the hall at {place} said that baths were on Saturdays and the hot water was by arrangement.

prop.text: a sign about baths on Saturdays
pay: I read the sign about the bath again on the way out. Saturday seemed a long way off.
The sign in the hall still said the hot water was by arrangement. Everything in this city is.
The sign about the bath had the last word in the hall, the way signs in rooming houses always do.

text: The stair at {place} had a brass rod on every step, and one of them was loose.

prop.text: a loose brass stair rod
pay: The loose stair rod caught my heel on the way down, as it had been waiting to all night.
I stepped over the loose stair rod. You learn a house by its traps.
The loose stair rod rattled behind me like a parting remark.

text: A coal merchant’s calendar hung by the stove at {place}, still turned to last month.

prop.text: a coal merchant’s calendar still turned to last month
pay: The calendar by the stove was still on last month. Nobody was going to turn it now.
I looked at the coal merchant’s calendar on my way out. It had stopped keeping track, and nobody was going to remind it.
The calendar went on saying last month. In that room, it might as well.

text: A radiator under the window at {place} knocked every so often, as if it wanted to be let in on something.

prop.text: a radiator that knocked
pay: The radiator knocked as I left. I didn’t answer it.
The radiator was still knocking. It was the only thing in the room with anything to say.
The radiator knocked twice behind me, which I took as a goodbye.

text: An empty birdcage hung in the corner at {place}, with nothing in it but a little swing.

prop.text: an empty birdcage with a little swing in it
pay: The little swing in the empty birdcage moved when I opened the door. That was all that moved.
I left the empty birdcage where it was. Some things in a room are only there to be sad.
The empty birdcage watched me go. It had been empty a long time and was used to it.

text: An aspidistra in a brass pot stood in the corner of {place}, dusted leaf by leaf.

prop.text: an aspidistra dusted leaf by leaf
pay: The aspidistra in the corner shone, leaf by leaf. It was the best-kept thing in the room, and it knew it.
I said goodbye to the aspidistra. It took it well.
The aspidistra in the corner hadn’t moved, which is the great thing about aspidistras.

text: There was an upright piano at {place} with a lace runner on top and photographs standing along it like a family on a station platform.

prop.text: an upright piano with photographs along the top
pay: The photographs on the piano watched me out, the whole family, unconvinced.
I passed the piano and didn’t touch it. It looked like the kind that remembers.
The piano stood with its photographs as if it were about to play something sad and had thought better of it.

text: A china shepherdess stood on a doily at {place}, looking at the room with painted patience.

prop.text: a china shepherdess on a doily
pay: The china shepherdess had kept her painted patience through all of it. I was running low on mine.
I nodded to the china shepherdess on the way out. She didn’t have any sheep either.
The china shepherdess went on minding her doily. Some jobs are small and you do them anyway.

text: A framed sampler on the wall at {place} said Bless This House in red cross-stitch.

prop.text: a framed sampler that said Bless This House
pay: Bless This House, said the sampler. It hadn’t said anything about the people coming into it.
I read the sampler again on my way out. It was asking a lot.
The sampler went on blessing the house in red cross-stitch, whatever the house was up to.

text: A supply company’s calendar hung behind the counter at {place}, with every day crossed off in pencil.

prop.text: a calendar with every day crossed off
pay: Another day would be crossed off that calendar tomorrow. I hoped it went easier than this one.
The crossed-off calendar behind the counter looked at me like a bill.
I left the calendar to its crossing off. It knew where it stood, which made one of us.

text: A bell on a spring hung over the door at {place}, and it rang when I came in as if it had been waiting all day.

prop.text: a bell on a spring over the door
pay: The bell over the door rang me out, as cheerful as if I’d bought something.
I went out under the bell. It rang anyway. It rings for everybody; that’s its trouble.
The bell over the door gave one more little ring, which is more of a send-off than I usually get.

text: A brass scale with a set of little weights stood at one end of the counter at {place}, perfectly balanced.

prop.text: a brass scale, perfectly balanced
pay: The brass scale at the end of the counter was still perfectly balanced. It was the only thing in the place that was.
I looked at the brass scale on the way out. Everything weighs something, if you have the little weights.
The scale stayed level as I passed. It had never had to weigh a night like this one.

text: A potted geranium sat in the window at {place}, red and stubborn, the only thing in the room that wasn’t there for business.

prop.text: a stubborn red geranium in the window
pay: The geranium in the window was still red and still stubborn. I took it as an example.
I passed the geranium on the way out. It had nothing to do with anything, which I envied.
The geranium went on being red in the window, whatever anybody thought about it.

text: A notice board by the stairs at {place} was covered in pinned papers three deep, all curling at the corners.

prop.text: a notice board pinned three deep
pay: The notice board by the stairs had one more curl at the corners than when I came in.
I read the notice board on the way out. Nothing pinned to it was any help.
Somewhere under three layers on the notice board there was probably something important. That’s how notice boards work, and nights.

text: A coffee urn stood by the wall at {place}, dented on one side and never off the boil.

prop.text: a dented coffee urn that was never off the boil
pay: The coffee urn by the wall was still boiling. It would be boiling when the rest of us were gone.
I could smell the urn coffee all the way down the stairs. It was strong enough to follow me home.
The urn by the wall had made a lot of coffee tonight, and none of it for me.

text: An electric fan turned slowly overhead at {place}, moving the warm air from one side of the room to the other and back.

prop.text: a slow electric fan overhead
pay: The fan overhead was still moving the air around without improving it. I knew the feeling.
I left the fan to its work. It had been at it longer than I had and got about as far.
The fan turned over my head once more as I went, like a slow nod.

text: A No Smoking sign hung on the wall at {place}, with a cigarette burn in the middle of it.

prop.text: a No Smoking sign with a cigarette burn in it
pay: The No Smoking sign still had its cigarette burn. Signs in this city are mostly suggestions.
I lit up on the stairs, under the No Smoking sign. It was used to it.
The No Smoking sign watched me go with its one burnt eye.

text: A bare bulb hung on a cord at {place}, swinging a little whenever the door shut.

prop.text: a bare bulb on a cord
pay: The bare bulb swung a little as I shut the door behind me, and the shadows changed their minds.
The bulb on its cord gave the place all the light it was going to get, which wasn’t much.
I left the bare bulb to light a room that didn’t want it.

text: An old tin sign for a cough syrup nobody makes any more was nailed to the wall at {place}.

prop.text: an old tin sign for a cough syrup nobody makes any more
pay: The tin sign was still promising relief. It had been promising it for years.
I read the old cough syrup sign on the way out. Relief guaranteed. I’d have settled for less.
The tin sign on the wall had outlasted the company and would outlast me.

text: An old radiator at {place} gave off a great deal more noise than heat.

prop.text: a radiator with more noise than heat
pay: The radiator banged twice on my way out, which was its idea of a conversation.
The radiator at least was honest about how little it had to offer.
I left the radiator to its banging. It had more to say than I did.

text: A wooden chair with one short leg stood by the wall at {place}, and rocked whenever anything touched it.

prop.text: a wooden chair with one short leg
prop.short: the chair with the short leg
pay: The chair with the short leg rocked once as I passed, as if it wanted a word.
I didn’t sit in the chair with the short leg. I was unsteady enough.
The short-legged chair went on rocking by the wall, getting nowhere in particular.

text: A kettle sat on a gas ring on the shelf at {place}, gone cold.

prop.text: a kettle on a gas ring
pay: The kettle on the gas ring was cold. Nobody was going to offer me tea in that flat.
I looked at the kettle on the way out. It looked back, empty and patient.
The kettle sat on its gas ring, a promise of tea that nobody meant to keep.

text: The wallpaper roses at {place} had faded to the colour of weak tea, except in the corners the light never reached.

prop.text: wallpaper roses faded to the colour of weak tea
pay: The faded roses on the wallpaper saw me out. They’d had better years too.
I took one more look at the wallpaper roses. Faded, but still trying. I could sympathise.
The wallpaper roses had given up on being red long ago and settled for being there.

text: A gramophone with a big tin horn stood in the corner at {place}, with a record still on it.

prop.text: a gramophone with a tin horn
pay: The gramophone in the corner kept its record to itself. I wasn’t in the mood for a tune anyway.
I passed the gramophone and left it alone. Some nights don’t need music.
The gramophone’s big tin horn pointed at me as I left, as if it had something to add.

text: There was a biscuit tin on the shelf at {place} with the King of England on the lid, looking unimpressed.

prop.text: a biscuit tin with the King of England on the lid
prop.short: the King on the biscuit tin
pay: The King on the biscuit tin was still unimpressed. I’d been trying all night.
I nodded to the King on the biscuit tin on my way out. He didn’t nod back. They never do.
The King on the biscuit tin kept his opinion to himself, which is what kings are for.

text: A cracked mirror over the washstand at {place} gave anybody who looked in it two faces.

prop.text: a cracked mirror over the washstand
pay: I caught both my faces in the cracked mirror on the way out. Neither looked rested.
The cracked mirror went on giving everybody two faces. In this city, that’s generous.
I didn’t look in the cracked mirror again. One face of mine is plenty.

text: A string of onions hung from a nail by the stove at {place}, and the whole room smelled faintly of them.

prop.text: a string of onions on a nail
pay: The onions on their nail were the most honest thing in the room. You always know where you are with an onion.
I left with the smell of the onions on my coat. It would stay longer than I had.
The string of onions swung a little as I shut the door, saying goodbye the only way it knew.

text: The ceiling at {place} sloped down so low on one side that a tall man would have to bow to the bed.

prop.text: a sloping ceiling
pay: I ducked under the sloping ceiling on my way out and still hit my head. It was that kind of night.
The sloping ceiling saw me off with a knock on the hat.
I bowed to the sloping ceiling one more time. It insisted.

text: A little iron stove at {place} had a crooked pipe that went up through the ceiling at an angle nobody would have chosen.

prop.text: an iron stove with a crooked pipe
pay: The crooked stovepipe went on up through the ceiling at its own angle. I admired that.
The stove ticked as it cooled. It had done its bit for the night.
I left the stove and its crooked pipe to keep the room warm without me.
